title: The history of understanding cloudbursts
tagline: From a word for a bursting cloud to radars on Himalayan ridges: how people learned what a cloudburst really is, and how to get out of its way.
intro: For two centuries people have pictured a cloud splitting open like a bag of water. Rain gauges, aircraft and radar told a different story: rising air holds the rain up, and a storm that stays over one valley can drop a season's water in an hour. Floods at Hyderabad, Big Thompson, Mumbai, Leh and Kedarnath showed what that means on the ground. India now defines a cloudburst by a number, watches the mountains with Doppler radar, and can send a warning to every phone in a valley.

eras.name: A word and a rain gauge
eras.summary: People name the cloudburst before they understand it, and learn to measure rain the same way everywhere.

eras.name: Inside the storm
eras.summary: Radar and aircraft show how a thunderstorm works, record downpours are measured, and canyon floods teach people to climb.

eras.name: Lessons from Mumbai and the Himalaya
eras.summary: Mumbai, Leh and Kedarnath show how local and how deadly extreme rain can be, and Indian scientists start to count cloudbursts.

eras.name: Radars and warnings
eras.summary: Doppler radars go up in the mountains, flash flood guidance and phone alerts begin, and each new disaster tests what 'cloudburst' means.

events.title: Korea measures the rain
events.who: King Sejong's court; the idea is credited to Crown Prince Munjong
events.text: In 1441 the Joseon court began catching rain in a standing cylinder and measuring its depth. It was called the cheugugi. By 1442 a standard size had been set and gauges were sent out to the provinces.
events.why: You cannot say how hard it rained until everyone measures rain the same way.

events.title: The word 'cloudburst' appears
events.text: The word 'cloud-burst' turns up in American English by about 1817, by one dictionary's count. The Oxford English Dictionary's earliest example is from an English newspaper in 1836, and Merriam-Webster gives 1869. German has the same picture in its word Wolkenbruch. People imagined a cloud as a bag of water that splits open.
events.why: The name stuck, but the picture is wrong: a cloud is not a bag, and nothing bursts.

events.title: A country of volunteer rain watchers
events.text: George Symons published the first volume of British Rainfall in 1860, with readings from a small group of observers. He kept asking for volunteers and testing gauges, and the network grew into the British Rainfall Organisation, with thousands of gauges across the British Isles.
events.why: A cloudburst is small. Only a dense net of gauges has a chance of catching one.

events.title: 206 mm in 20 minutes
events.text: A storm over the town of Curtea de Arges is listed with 206 mm of rain in 20 minutes. More than a century later it is still the greatest 20 minute fall on the US National Weather Service's world list.
events.why: It showed how much water a single storm can drop on one spot in the time of a school break.

events.title: The Musi floods Hyderabad
events.text: After two days of very heavy rain, and a downpour at dawn that many accounts call a cloudburst, small reservoirs upstream gave way and the Musi river rose through the old city. About 15,000 people are commonly said to have died, and some accounts give higher figures. Reports of the rainfall differ: one widely quoted figure is about 17 inches (430 mm) in 36 hours. The Nizam's government asked the engineer M. Visvesvaraya for a plan. He reported in 1909, and two flood reservoirs followed: Osman Sagar in 1920 and Himayat Sagar in 1927.
events.why: It is the flood that made an Indian city plan for extreme rain, with reservoirs upstream and a rebuilt riverfront.

events.title: Radar sees a shower
events.text: Wartime radar was built to find aircraft, but rain kept showing up on the screens. On 20 February 1941 a 10 cm radar on the English coast tracked a shower about 7 miles out to sea. It is the earliest well recorded case of radar following rain.
events.why: Radar can watch rain falling between the gauges, which is where most cloudbursts happen.

events.title: The Thunderstorm Project
events.text: Pilots flew radar-equipped P-61 aircraft straight through thunderstorms, five at a time, stacked at different heights. Horace Byers led the project and Roscoe Braham was its senior analyst. Their 1949 report showed that a storm is made of cells, and each cell lives through three stages: a growing stage that is all updraft, a mature stage with heavy rain and a downdraft, and a fading stage.
events.why: It replaced the bursting bag with the real story: rising air holds the water up, and the rain comes down when the updraft can no longer carry it.

events.title: Holt, Missouri: 305 mm in 42 minutes
events.text: On a Sunday evening a line of storms dropped about 12 inches (305 mm) of rain on the small town of Holt in 42 minutes. The World Meteorological Organization lists it as the greatest rainfall known within one hour. The figure came from a careful survey after the storm, not from an automatic gauge.
events.why: It is the yardstick: about three times the rate that India's weather department uses to define a cloudburst.

events.title: The wettest minute
events.text: A gauge at Unionville in Maryland recorded 31.2 mm of rain in one minute on 4 July 1956. The World Meteorological Organization lists it as the world record for one minute. The US National Weather Service list also carries 38 mm in one minute at Barot, Guadeloupe, on 26 November 1970.
events.why: Rain can fall, for a moment, more than 15 times faster than the cloudburst threshold. It just cannot keep that up.

events.title: The Alaknanda flood
events.where: Alaknanda valley, between Joshimath and Chamoli, Uttarakhand
events.text: A flood on the night of 20 July 1970 has been attributed to a cloudburst on the mountain front of the Alaknanda valley. Landslides dammed side streams and then broke. The roadside settlement of Belakuchi was washed away along with a convoy of about 30 buses, and what was left of the Gohna lake of 1894 was wiped out. Later studies linked the damage to heavy commercial tree felling on the slopes.
events.why: Villagers drew the link between bare slopes and floods, and the Chipko movement began in the same valley in 1973.

events.title: The Rapid City flood
events.where: Rapid City and the Black Hills, South Dakota
events.text: Thunderstorms stalled against the Black Hills and dropped as much as 15 inches (380 mm) of rain in about six hours near Nemo. Rapid Creek rose through the city in the night and Canyon Lake Dam failed. The Red Cross counted 238 dead and about 3,000 injured.
events.why: Rapid City turned its floodplain into parkland so that people would not live in the river's path again.

events.title: 401 mm in one hour
events.text: The US National Weather Service's world list gives 401 mm of rain in 60 minutes at Shangdi in Inner Mongolia. It is the largest one hour figure on that list. The World Meteorological Organization's own archive still names Holt for the one hour record.
events.why: Record lists differ because extreme rain at a single point is so hard to measure and to check.

events.title: The Big Thompson Canyon flood
events.text: A thunderstorm sat almost still over the upper canyon on a holiday evening. About 7.5 inches (190 mm) fell in roughly an hour, and about 12 inches (300 mm) in a few hours. A surge of water ran down the narrow canyon and 144 people died. Researchers found that many who survived had left their cars and climbed the hillside.
events.why: Colorado put up 'Climb to safety' signs in its canyons: in a flash flood you go up, not along the road.

events.title: A Doppler radar net over a whole country
events.text: The first NEXRAD Doppler weather radar for daily forecasting was installed at Sterling, Virginia, on 12 June 1992. The last of the original network went in at North Webster, Indiana, on 30 August 1997. About 160 radars now cover the country and estimate rainfall every few minutes.
events.why: Forecasters could watch a storm stall over one valley and warn people downstream within minutes.

events.title: The ingredients of a flash flood
events.who: Charles Doswell, Harold Brooks and Robert Maddox
events.text: Three American meteorologists set out a simple rule in the journal Weather and Forecasting. The rain a place gets is the rain rate multiplied by how long it lasts. So the heaviest totals come where rain is intense and the storm stays put, or where new cells keep passing over the same spot. Forecasters should look for the ingredients: moisture, rising air and slow storm movement.
events.why: It gave forecasters everywhere the same checklist, and it explains why a stalled storm is the dangerous one.

events.title: Mumbai: 944 mm in a day
events.text: The Santacruz observatory recorded 944 mm of rain in the 24 hours to 8:30 the next morning. Between 2:30 and 3:30 in the afternoon the rate passed 190 mm in an hour, well above the 100 mm mark for a cloudburst. Colaba, about 27 km away, had only 73 mm. Almost 419 people died in the city, and about 1,000 across Maharashtra.
events.why: It showed that cloudburst-scale rain is not only a mountain problem: the city's old drains were built for about 25 mm an hour.

events.title: Leh, Ladakh
events.text: Around midnight a short, violent storm hit the bare slopes above Leh, a cold desert that normally gets about 100 mm of rain in a year. Mud and boulders ran down the stream beds into Choglamsar and other villages. The official count is at least 255 dead, and some studies put the toll near 600. The airport gauge caught only 12.8 mm. Scientists who read the damage estimated at least 75 mm in 30 minutes in a band about 6 km wide, and one study estimated up to about 250 mm in an hour.
events.why: The storm missed the only gauge, so its size had to be worked out afterwards from the scars it left.

events.title: Kedarnath
events.text: The monsoon arrived early and met a western weather system over Uttarakhand. A research station at Chorabari glacier, above Kedarnath, measured 325 mm of rain in 24 hours. On the morning of 17 June the loose moraine bank holding back Chorabari lake gave way and a second surge hit the temple town. The state government said in July 2013 that more than 5,700 people were presumed dead, and later counts are above 6,000.
events.why: It was widely called a cloudburst, but it was days of extreme rain over a large area plus a lake breach: the label hides the cause.

events.title: A review of Himalayan cloudbursts
events.who: A. P. Dimri and seven co-authors
events.text: A. P. Dimri and colleagues gathered what was known about cloudbursts in the Indian Himalaya in the journal Earth-Science Reviews. They described how moist monsoon air is forced up steep slopes, how storms can be trapped in narrow valleys, and how few instruments there are where these storms strike.
events.why: It set out plainly how little is measured, and what radars and gauges the mountains need.

events.title: The 'mini cloudburst' gets a name
events.who: N. R. Deshpande, D. R. Kothawale, V. Kumar and J. R. Kulkarni
events.where: Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune
events.text: India's weather department calls it a cloudburst when a station gets 10 cm (100 mm) of rain in one hour. Scientists at IITM Pune studied hourly rain from 126 stations for 1969 to 2015. They added a second class, the mini cloudburst: 5 cm or more in two hours in a row. They counted about 200 of these a year, with a rising trend along the Himalayan foothills and the west coast.
events.why: A strict line misses many dangerous storms, so a second, lower line helps to count and study them.

events.title: Flash flood guidance for South Asia
events.who: India Meteorological Department and the World Meteorological Organization
events.text: India launched the South Asia Flash Flood Guidance System, serving Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal and Sri Lanka. It combines rain estimates and soil wetness for small watersheds on a 4 km grid. It gives a flash flood threat for the next 6 hours and a risk for the next 24.
events.why: The warning is about the stream, not only the sky: the same rain is far more dangerous on ground that is already soaked.

events.title: Doppler radars for the Himalaya
events.where: Mukteshwar, Uttarakhand, and Kufri, Himachal Pradesh
events.text: On the weather department's 146th foundation day, Doppler radars at Mukteshwar and Kufri were dedicated to the nation. More followed: Jammu on 5 September 2021, Leh on 14 January 2022, and on 15 January 2023 Surkanda Devi in Uttarakhand, Murari Devi and Jot in Himachal Pradesh, and Banihal Top in Jammu and Kashmir. Lansdowne in Uttarakhand was added on 23 February 2024. Each of the small mountain radars sees about 100 km around it.
events.why: A gauge sees one point. A radar can see a storm building over a valley that has no gauge at all.

events.title: Chamoli: not a cloudburst
events.where: Ronti Peak, Rishiganga and Dhauliganga valleys, Uttarakhand
events.text: On a clear winter morning a flood of water, ice and rock tore down the Rishiganga valley and wrecked two hydropower projects. More than 200 people were killed or are missing. A study in Science by a large international team showed that about 27 million cubic metres of rock and glacier ice had fallen from Ronti Peak.
events.why: Not every sudden mountain flood starts with rain, so the cause has to be checked before it is named.

events.title: Amarnath: a flood without a 'cloudburst'
events.where: Near the Amarnath cave shrine, Jammu and Kashmir
events.text: At about 5:30 in the evening water and debris swept through a camp of pilgrims below the cave. At least 16 people died and dozens were reported missing. The weather department said its station at the shrine had measured 31 mm between 4:30 and 6:30, far short of 100 mm in an hour. It said the flood was probably caused by very local rain higher up the mountain.
events.why: Light rain where you stand tells you little about the stream beside you, which is fed from slopes above.

events.title: Himachal Pradesh's monsoon
events.where: Shimla, Solan, Kullu and Mandi districts, Himachal Pradesh
events.text: Two spells of extreme rain, in early July and in mid August, set off floods and hundreds of landslides. On 14 August a slope gave way at Summer Hill in Shimla and buried the Shiv Bawdi temple: 20 people died. The same day a reported cloudburst at Jadon village in Solan killed seven. The state's emergency centre counted 428 deaths between 24 June and mid September.
events.why: Most of the lives were lost to slopes and streams, not to the rain itself: where people build decides the toll.

events.title: South Lhonak: a lake, not a cloud
events.where: South Lhonak lake and the Teesta valley, Sikkim
events.text: Around midnight the moraine bank of South Lhonak glacial lake failed, and a flood ran down the Teesta. It destroyed the dam of the 1,200 MW Teesta III hydropower project at Chungthang. Early reports spoke of a cloudburst. Studies since have traced it to a collapse of frozen moraine into the lake, which sent a wave over the bank.
events.why: A glacial lake outburst and a cloudburst look alike from downstream, but they need different watching.

events.title: Dharali
events.text: At about 1:30 in the afternoon a wall of mud and rock came down the Kheer Gad stream and buried much of Dharali's market. Early official counts were low, with dozens missing: later reports say about 70 people are dead or presumed dead. Officials first called it a cloudburst. Nearby gauges had recorded only light rain, and scientists are still studying the cause. One reading is that rain set off slides in loose glacial debris high up, which turned into a debris flow.
events.why: The market stood on the fan of debris that the stream itself had built: the stream came back to it.

events.title: Chashoti, Kishtwar
events.where: Chashoti (also spelled Chositi), Kishtwar district, Jammu and Kashmir
events.text: At about 11:30 in the morning a flash flood reported as a cloudburst hit the last roadside village on the Machail Mata pilgrimage route. A community kitchen full of pilgrims was swept away. Counts by officials rose to at least 65 dead, with dozens more missing. There was no gauge on the slope above, so the rain rate itself is not known.
events.why: Pilgrim camps sit beside mountain streams in the peak of the monsoon, which is exactly where and when flash floods come.

events.title: Alerts that reach every phone in an area
events.who: Department of Telecommunications, C-DOT and NDMA
events.text: India launched a cell broadcast alert system with a nationwide test message. It is built by C-DOT and joined to SACHET, the disaster authority's alert platform, which uses the international Common Alerting Protocol and had already sent billions of SMS warnings. A cell broadcast goes to every phone in the chosen area at once and sounds even on silent.
events.why: A cloudburst warning has minutes to work, so it has to reach people without anyone dialling a number.

series.title: Rain measured in an hour or less in this story
series.caption: Five measured or surveyed bursts, each lasting an hour or less. India's weather department calls 100 mm in an hour a cloudburst.

points.label: Curtea de Arges, Romania: 206 mm in 20 minutes
Shangdi, Inner Mongolia: 401 mm in 1 hour
Big Thompson, Colorado: about 190 mm in about 1 hour
Santacruz, Mumbai: just over 190 mm in 1 hour

facts: India's weather department has a one-line test: if a station gets 10 cm of rain in one hour, it is a cloudburst.
On 26 July 2005 Santacruz in Mumbai recorded 944 mm of rain in 24 hours. Colaba, about 27 km away, recorded 73 mm.
The wettest minute in the World Meteorological Organization's archive is 31.2 mm, at Unionville, Maryland, in 1956.
Leh normally gets about 100 mm of rain in a whole year. In 2010 its airport gauge recorded just 12.8 mm while a storm a few kilometres away destroyed villages.
At the Amarnath shrine in 2022 the gauge showed 31 mm in two hours, yet a deadly flood came down the stream from higher up.
After the 1976 Big Thompson flood, Colorado put up road signs in its canyons that say: Climb to safety.
